WWP Summary Decision
BACKGROUND
The Devil Creek Group I Final Decisions on appeal herein were preceded
historically by lengthy litigation between Appellant, Western Watersheds Project
(“WWP”), and the Respondent, Bureau of Land Management (“BLM”). The Jarbidge
Field Office covers some 1.7 million acres of public and private lands in south/central
Idaho. Prior to 2015, the 1987 Jarbidge Resource Management Plan covered the
10

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
allotments that are the subject of the instant Group 1 consolidated appeals, referenced
by docket numbers above. Beginning in 2004, BLM began issuing a number of
temporary non-renewable (“TNR”) grazing permits which did not include
environmental analyses, nor public comment. BLM was administratively preparing
some five Environmental Assessments (“EA”), but the TNRs were issued without the
support of EAs.
Subsequently, WWP sued BLM in the Federal District Court for the District of
Idaho, alleging that the grazing increases included in the TNRs violated NEPA and
FLPMA. The court subsequently issued a decision in WWP’s favor determining that the
TNR permits were unlawfully issued and ultimately issued an injunction, which
terminated grazing on some 28 allotments until BLM issued a new EIS, as well as, new
grazing decisions., WWP v. Bennett, Case No. 1:04-cv-00181-BLW, ECF No. 67 (D. Idaho
Aug. 25, 2004), pp. 24-27. Subsequently, WWP, BLM, Simplot Livestock Company and
Brackett Ranches, Inc. executed a Stipulated Settlement Agreement on September 30,
2005, which was approved by the court. Thereunder, BLM was to prepare a full EIS
covering the entire Jarbidge Resource Area, which was to be the basis for revising and
updating the Jarbidge RMP and for the ultimate issuance of new grazing decisions.
BLM invited scoping comments with respect to amendments of the RMP and conducted
range studies in 2006. In March 2007, BLM issued its “Analysis of the Management
Situation for the Jarbidge Resource Management Plan” (“Jarbidge AMS”). BER 014638-
015018.
Then, in 2007 the Murphy Complex Fire burned some 426,000 acres within the
area of the Jarbidge Field Office, 64 % of which were in the Devil Creek Subregion.
Revised EA, p. 132; BER 042616. The fire had major impacts upon vegetation and
wildlife, including sage-grouse nesting habitats and sage-grouse leks. That fire was
followed by the Long Butte Fire and the 2012 Kinyon Road Fire, and largely, as a result
of those interruptions, BLM did not issue its Record of Decision for the revised Jarbidge
RMP until September 2015, which was then followed by the multi-state Approved
Resource Management Plan Amendments for Sage-Grouse (“2015 ARMPA”).
In the updated Jarbidge RMP, BLM increased the number of AUMs from 189,000
in the 1987 RMP to some 326,000 AUMs in the 2015 RMP. This was done based on data
reflecting large quantities of available forage for livestock under the vegetation
allocations, but with low levels of utilization. 2015 Jarbidge RMP, pp. 18-19; BER
018847-48. BLM and the U.S. Forest Service developed the 2015 ARMPA in response to
the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service determination in 2010 under the Endangered Species
Act that listing Greater Sage-grouse was warranted but precluded for listing because of
higher government priorities. 75 Fed. Reg. 13910, March 23, 2010. The Idaho ARMPA
11

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
established a three-tier management system for sage-grouse habitat based upon relative
habitat importance, as follows: (1) priority habitat management areas (“PHMA”),
which have the highest habitat value for maintaining sustainable sage-grouse
populations; (2) important habitat management areas (“IHMA”), which provide a
buffer for and which connect PHNA’s; and, (3) general habitat management areas
(“GHMA”), which are occupied seasonally or year-round outside of PHMAs. 2015
Record of Decision, pp. 2-8; BER 017009. The management areas are based on the State
of Idaho’s key habitat maps, which identify areas necessary for sage-grouse
conservation. BER 010710-711. Most of the Devil Creek Subregion is mapped as IHMA.
Revised EA, pp. 151-152; BER 042635-36. Because the relevant triggers in the 2015
ARMPA have been exceeded, the IHMA areas are actually managed by BLM as if they
were PHMA areas. Ibid.
In order to process new grazing permits, in 2016 the Jarbidge Field Office
divided its 1.7 million-acre territory into subregions, based upon similar topography
and related management issues. The Devil Creek Subregion was the first to be analyzed
by BLM under the auspices of the Devil Creek Subregion Livestock Grazing Permit
Renewal EA, which covers 29 separate allotments including some 357,806 acres of land.
Revised EA, p. 122; BER 042606. In preparing its EA, BLM analyzed rangeland health
data gathered between 2012 and 2016, which was incorporated into rangeland health
assessments in 2017, which, in turn, became the bases for the alternatives that were
analyzed in the Revised EA. Revised EA, pp. 2-4, BER 042485-042487. BLM analyzed
six alternatives in detail, and an additional three in lesser detail, in order to assess the
impacts of fires and livestock grazing over a period of time. The six main alternatives
analyzed were the following: (1) a no action alternative which implicated a
continuation of the previously existing management scheme; (2) the permittee
proposed management schemes; (3) management based on vegetation production; (4)
management based on vegetation production modified to include resource limitations;
(5) a reduction in grazing levels; and, (6) a no grazing option. Revised EA, pp. 12-15;
BER 041812-15. The alternatives considered, but not analyzed in detail were the
following: (1) infrastructure projects, such as, wells, water pipelines, and fences; (2)
deferment of grazing schedules; and, (3) changes in seasons of use. Revised EA. Pp.
114-116; BER 041914-16.
On August 21, 2019, BLM published the Proposed EA along with the Proposed
Decisions for all of the subject subregion allotments. Generally speaking, the field
manager determined that wildfire-related conditions could be improved over the
course of the ten-year permits by increasing livestock grazing levels in areas where non-
native grass species crowded out native vegetation, thereby allowing sagebrush
communities to re-expand. BLM received 12 protests of the Proposed Decisions from
12

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
grazing permittees, two protests from WWP and Wildlands Defense, and one protest
from the Idaho Cattle Association. In response, BLM amended the Proposed EA,
resulting in the Revised EA issued on February 28, 2020, with its accompanying FONSI.
Revised EA, pp. 2-3; BER 042485-042486. The Final Decisions for seventeen of the
subject allotments were issued on February 28, 2020. The Final Decisions for the
remaining eleven allotments in Group 2 were issued on June 15, 2020.
STANDARD OF SUMMARY JUDGMENT REVIEW
To obtain Summary Judgment there must be no substantive, material issue of
fact in dispute, and the issues for adjudication must be legal in content. Larson v. BLM,
129 IBLA 250, 252 (1994). Generally speaking, the Departmental Cases Hearings
Division, as well as, the Interior Board of Land Appeals, follow the rules of summary
judgment set out under Rule 56 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, under which all
factual inferences must be drawn in the light most favorable to the non-moving party,
drawing all reasonable inferences in its favor. Dannelle and Chad Hensley, et al., 195
IBLA 345, 354 (2020). Summary judgment is authorized where the evidence establishes
that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and where the moving party is
entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Anderson v.Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242,
247 (1986).
Once the moving party has met its burden, the burden then shifts to the non-
moving party to set forth by affidavit, or other means, specific facts showing that there
is a genuine issue of material fact or that, legally, the moving party is not entitled to
judgment. T.W. Electric Service Inc. v. Pacific Electric Contractors Association, 809 F.2d
626, 630 (9th Cir. 1987). Legal memoranda are not evidence and do not create issues of
fact capable of defeating an otherwise valid motion for summary judgment. British
Airways Board v. Boeing Company, 585 F.2d 946, 952 (9th Cir. 1987).
CONTENTIONS OF WWP
With respect to the relationship between grazing, invasive species and wildfires,
WWP states the following, “Grazing has many impacts on sage-steppe ecology and
wildlife, both widespread and localized. However, the most significant long-term
impacts result from the interaction between grazing, invasive annual grasses, and
wildfire. Livestock grazing makes sage-steppe communities more susceptible to
wildfire and annual grass invasion by suppressing native bunchgrasses, and by
damaging biological soil crusts.” WWP’s Opening Summary Judgment Brief (“WWP
SJM”), p. 18; citing the Declaration of J. Boone Kauffman, Para. 10. Generally speaking,
WWP disagrees with BLM’s determination that sage-steppe ecosystems within the
13

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
Devil Creek Subregion are grazing adapted and that the grazing increases approved in
the subject Final Decisions will help to restore native vegetation. WWP argues to the
contrary that livestock grazing causes cheatgrass dominance of sage-steppe ecosystems,
and, relatedly, WWP contends that wildfires convert native sage-steppe and native
grasslands into invasive annual grasslands. WWP SJM, p. 20; Kauffman Declaration,
Para. 16. It is further argued that conversion of native vegetation to cheatgrass caused
by heavy livestock grazing has catastrophic impacts upon sage-grouse. WWP SJM, p.
21; Kauffman Declaration, Para. 20.
Noting that there are some 688 miles of fences within the Devil Creek Subregion,
WWP argues that impacts from fences include loss of birds through collisions,
fragmentation of habitat, habitat degradation, spread of invasive plants, and increased
perching opportunities for ravens and other predators. WWP SJM, p. 25. With respect
to riparian habitats it is contended that excessive grazing degrades riparian habitats by
changing, reducing, or eliminating vegetation. WWP SJM, p. 27; Kauffman Declaration,
Para. 27.
WWP disagrees with BLM’s basic policy determination that increased grazing in
the subregion is an effective strategy for reducing the risk of wildfire. In particular,
WWP argues the following:
The Devil Creek Group 1 Final Decisions authorize as much as 40-60%
utilization on allotments across the subregion, which is far greater than
the 25% utilization recommended for the arid West by range science
experts, and also greater than the 25-30% recommended by sage-grouse
experts. The 40-60% forage utilization authorized by BLM in the Devil
Creek Final Decision will, over the 10-year term of the grazing permits
constitute chronic overgrazing that will promote the expansion of
cheatgrass and exacerbate the livestock-cheatgrass-fire cycle … . Because
of the high utilization rates required to influence wildlife behavior,
intensive grazing for wildfire control and prevention is especially harmful
if used within intact sage-steppe habitat. At the same time, permitted
grazing with a 40-60% utilization ceiling will not significantly alter fire
behavior in the hot, dry conditions typical of fire seasons in the
intermountain West.
BLM asserts that by reducing ‘fuels’ through grazing, it is possible to
prevent or control large wildfires. However, fuels are only one of three
factors influencing fire behavior. The other two factors—weather and
topography—contribute significantly to wildfire intensity and rate of
14

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
spread. During the hot dry fire seasons characteristic of the intermountain
West, the combination of high winds, high temperatures, and low relative
humidity often lead to ‘extreme’ conditions under which fuels reductions
are not effective. Thus, grazing to reduce fuel loads will not effectively
control large wildfires.
WWP SJM, pp. 30-31; citing to Kauffman Declaration, Paras. 33, 35.
WWP contends that the subject Final Decisions contain no terms, conditions or
other directives intended to protect, restore or enhance soil crusts, and the invasion of
cheatgrass is also a substantial concern. WWP SJM, p. 32. WWP further contends that
the Final Decisions contain no terms, conditions, or thresholds intended to protect
pastures still having a significant portion of sage-steppe, other than the utilization levels
specified in those decisions, which WWP contends are inadequate for that purpose.
WWP SJM, p. 33. Relatedly, WWP contends that BLM failed to include measures to
protect some 280,767 acres of big game winter range. Ibid. WWP criticizes the
authorization of “year-round” grazing on most of the subject allotments, and argues
that “… BLM has increased grazing by over 200% while loosening restrictions on
grazing permittees.” Ibid. This would allegedly result in an increase in the “… already
inflated livestock use, up to a maximum of 45,265 AUMs across 15 of the 24 Group 1
allotments.” Ibid.
WWP argues that management guidelines are provided exclusively for forage
utilization levels without including habitat-related standards, guidelines, or thresholds
as required in the 2015 ARMPA. WWP SJM, p. 34. Monitoring requirements are
contended to be inadequate, because, “At most BLM will monitor utilization and
herbaceous cover once every three years. But this frequent (relatively speaking)
monitoring is provided for on only nine allotments. On the others, monitoring will
occur on a five-year interval, or longer. In many cases, BLM is required to monitor only
utilization and herbaceous cover. More in-depth monitoring methods and assessments
of the functioning condition of riparian areas are called for only once every ten years.”
Ibid. WWP points out that none of the allotments in Group 1 are meeting all applicable
standards for rangeland health, contending that in many cases grazing is the primary
cause. WWP SJM, p. 35.
Based upon the above-referenced considerations, WWP argues that the Group 1
decisions required the preparation of a full-EIS, not just an EA. Contending that the
decisions implicate significant environmental impacts, WWP argues that the EA and
Decisions/FONSIs here violate NEPA, 42 U.S.C. 4321-4370h (2016), in several respects.
First, in light of the enormous area covered, resource values at stake, and uncertainty
15

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
about the effects of the new grazing regime, WWP argues that it was arbitrary and
capricious for BLM to conclude that the decisions would have “no significant impact;”
instead, a full EIS was required. Second, WWP argues that the EA failed to take a” hard
look” at the environmental impacts of the grazing and range improvements authorized.
Third, it is alleged that the final Revised EA does not present its analyses or conclusions
in a clear or understandable manner, and it is, therefore, allegedly difficult to tell which

DISCUSSION
With respect to NEPA compliance, Section 102(2)(C) requires consideration of the
potential impacts of a federal agency’s proposed action in a full EIS if that action is
“major” and “significantly” affects the quality of the environment. 42 U.S.C. 4332(2)(C).
A BLM decision approving an action based on an EA and FONSI will be approved if
BLM has taken the requisite “hard look” at the proposed action and identified relevant
areas of environmental concern such that it can make an informed determination that
the proposal’s impacts are insignificant or will be reduced to insignificance by the
adoption of appropriate mitigation measures. Oregon Chapter of the Sierra Club, 172
IBLA 27, 46-47 (2007); Biodiversity Conservation Alliance, 169 IBLA 321, 331 (2006). To
prevail in challenging BLM’s Final Decisions on NEPA grounds, WWP must prove by a
preponderance of the evidence that the Revised EA does not support the accompanying
FONSI because the EA contains an error of law, a demonstratable error of fact, or fails
to consider a substantial environmental question of material significance. Escalante
Wilderness Project v. BLM, 176 IBLA 300, 303 (2009); Wilderness Watch, 176 IBLA 75, 87
(2008). However, “Mere differences of opinion provide no basis for reversal of BLM’s
action if it is reasonable and supported by the record on appeal.” Smigel v. BLM, 155
IBLA 158, 166 (2001). BLM is required by Section 102(2)(E) of NEPA to consider
appropriate alternatives to its proposed action, as well as their environmental
consequences. Appropriate alternatives are defined by IBLA, as follows, “Appropriate
alternatives are those that are reasonable alternatives to the proposed action, will
accomplish its intended purpose, are technically and economically feasible, and yet
have a lesser or no impact.” The Wilderness Workshop, 175 IBLA 124, 135 (2008).
Similarly, IBLA has stated that, “A ‘rule of reason’ applies to both the range of
alternatives that must be considered and the extent to which each alternative must be
20

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
addressed.” Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 182 IBLA 377, 390-91 (2012); 40 C.F.R.
1500.2(e), 1508.9(b).
BLM enjoys broad discretion with respect to its management of public range
lands. This authority has been elucidated in numerous precedential decisions issued by
IBLA. Among those is the now-familiar test that a BLM grazing decision may be
reversed if and only if it is not supportable on any rational basis. Smigel, 155 IBLA at
164. Throughout their entire case-in-chief, WWP persists in the apparent presumption
that the “rational basis” test is a legal balancing test. It affirmatively is not a balancing
test, under which the presiding ALJ at the Hearings Division level (i.e. the trial level)
would enjoy the authority to weigh the views of conflicting experts and conflicting
documentary evidence and to conclude that the party with the higher percentage of
such evidence would win. The controlling IBLA precedent does not authorize the
undersigned to apply such a balancing test. To the contrary, if BLM proves “any
rational basis” for its grazing decision, then, under the Smigel precedent, the
undersigned is mandated to affirm BLM’s decision. And, upon close review, WWP’s
arguments constitute mere differences of opinion and differences of policy with respect
to the Final Decisions on appeal herein. WWP has presented insufficient evidence to
meet its burden of proof in a Taylor Grazing Act appeal, namely that it must prove its
case by a preponderance of the evidence. Kelly v. BLM, 131 IBLA 146 (1994); Eason v.
BLM, 127 IBLA 259, 262-63 (1993). As such, an Appellant must show not just that the
results of BLM’s analyses and ensuing conclusions could be in error, but that they are,
in fact, erroneous. BLM v. Western Watersheds Project, 191 IBLA 144, 180-181 (2017).
WWP has not met this test. And, under the Smigel “rational basis” test, I do not enjoy
the discretionary legal authority to reverse BLM’s Final Decisions on appeal herein,
because BLM proved a clear, rational basis for each of those decisions, namely, that the
increased grazing levels authorized in the Final Decisions would, in fact, reduce fine
fuels leading to a reduction in wildfires with resulting long-term improvement in range
conditions. Consequently, for these and related reasons discussed below, WWP’s
Motion For Summary Judgment must be denied.
Basically WWP’s appeal comes down to its underlying contention that only
substantial reductions in livestock grazing on the subject allotments will reduce the
continued expansion of cheatgrass and other noxious and invasive plants, thereby
allegedly fostering ecological conditions to generally improve with a related, ensuing
long, term reduction in wildfires. BLM, to the contrary, contends that its authorization
of grazing increases will serve to reduce so-called fine fuels, which will be grazed
down, thereby reducing the risk of wildfires that have historically plagued the Group 1
allotments. Burk Flat Allotment Final Decision (which is utilized as an exemplary model
decision re this and other issues on appeal herein) , pp. 43-71, BER 042813-042841.

intended to restore the resilience of sagebrush- steppe ecosystem structure and function
through restoration projects and enhanced wildfire management. BER 015129. The
selected alternative VI focuses on exactly that objective. In fact, BLM’s Final Decisions
in Group 1 employ increased livestock grazing as one tool intended to improve the
overall resiliency of the subregion sagebrush-steppe.
26

ID-JFO-2020-001 thru -034
WWP contends that BLM failed to comply with applicable rangeland health
regulations because it allegedly did not specify enforceable terms, conditions, or
management criteria that would contribute to the various allotments meeting or making
progress toward meeting applicable rangeland health standards. However, each of the
decisions includes grazing management criteria, including objectives, management
guidelines, thresholds, and typically a rotational grazing system (for example, Term
and Condition # 2 in the Buck Flat Allotment Final Decision). Buck Flat Allotment Final
Decision, p. 11, BER 042781.
CONCLUSION
The Jarbidge Field Manager relied upon the input and advice of the multi-person
interdisciplinary team that evaluated resources on the subject allotments and also
assisted in the drafting of the EA and FONSI. As IBLA has stated, “A party challenging
BLM’s reliance on the professional opinion of its experts must show their opinion to be
arbitrary and capricious or, by a preponderance of the evidence, that it was based on a
material error in methodology, data, analysis or conclusion. … Conclusory allegations
of error or a mere difference of professional opinion will not suffice to show BLM erred
in relying on the professional opinion of its experts.” BLM v. Western Watersheds
Project, 191 IBLA 144, 180-181 (2017).
Consequently, for the above-stated factual and legal reasons, WWP’s Motion For
Summary Judgment is DENIED; BLM’s Motion For Summary Judgment is GRANTED;
and BLM’s Final Decisions on appeal herein are APPROVED.
